claim: PIK3R1 encodes three regulatory subunits of class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K).
source: PIK3R1 encodes three regulatory subunits of class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), each associating with any of three catalytic subunits, namely p110α, p110β, or p110δ.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational fact about PIK3R1.

claim: Each PIK3R1 regulatory subunit can associate with any of three catalytic subunits: p110α, p110β, or p110δ.
source: PIK3R1 encodes three regulatory subunits of class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), each associating with any of three catalytic subunits, namely p110α, p110β, or p110δ.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the protein interactions.

claim: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in PIK3R1 cause SHORT syndrome.
source: Constitutional PIK3R1 mutations cause diseases with a genotype-phenotype relationship not yet fully explained: heterozygous loss-of-function mutations cause SHORT syndrome, featuring insulin resistance and short stature attributed to reduced p110α function
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: SHORT syndrome features insulin resistance and short stature attributed to reduced p110α function.
source: heterozygous loss-of-function mutations cause SHORT syndrome, featuring insulin resistance and short stature attributed to reduced p110α function
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of SHORT syndrome.

claim: Heterozygous activating mutations in PIK3R1 cause immunodeficiency known as APDS2.
source: while heterozygous activating mutations cause immunodeficiency, attributed to p110δ activation and known as APDS2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: APDS2 is attributed to p110δ activation.
source: while heterozygous activating mutations cause immunodeficiency, attributed to p110δ activation and known as APDS2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the mechanism underlying APDS2.

claim: APDS2 patients do not show features of p110α hyperactivation.
source: Surprisingly, APDS2 patients do not show features of p110α hyperactivation, but do commonly have SHORT syndrome-like features, suggesting p110α hypofunction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a surprising clinical observation.

claim: APDS2 patients commonly have SHORT syndrome-like features.
source: Surprisingly, APDS2 patients do not show features of p110α hyperactivation, but do commonly have SHORT syndrome-like features, suggesting p110α hypofunction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple case reports cited in the introduction.

claim: SHORT syndrome-like features in APDS2 patients suggest p110α hypofunction.
source: Surprisingly, APDS2 patients do not show features of p110α hyperactivation, but do commonly have SHORT syndrome-like features, suggesting p110α hypofunction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an interpretation of clinical observations.

claim: In dermal fibroblasts from an APDS2 patient, there was no increased PI3K signalling.
source: In dermal fibroblasts from an APDS2 patient, we found no increased PI3K signalling, with p110δ expression markedly reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by immunoblotting data in Figure 1.

claim: In dermal fibroblasts from an APDS2 patient, p110δ expression was markedly reduced.
source: In dermal fibroblasts from an APDS2 patient, we found no increased PI3K signalling, with p110δ expression markedly reduced.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: In preadipocytes, the APDS2 variant was potently dominant negative.
source: In preadipocytes, the APDS2 variant was potently dominant negative, associating with Irs1 and Irs2 but failing to heterodimerise with p110α.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2, 5, and 6.

claim: The APDS2 variant associates with Irs1 and Irs2.
source: In preadipocytes, the APDS2 variant was potently dominant negative, associating with Irs1 and Irs2 but failing to heterodimerise with p110α.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The APDS2 variant fails to heterodimerise with p110α.
source: In preadipocytes, the APDS2 variant was potently dominant negative, associating with Irs1 and Irs2 but failing to heterodimerise with p110α.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Attenuation of p110α signalling by a p110δ-activating PIK3R1 variant potentially explains co-incidence of gain-of-function and loss-of-function PIK3R1 phenotypes.
source: This attenuation of p110α signalling by a p110δ-activating PIK3R1 variant potentially explains co-incidence of gain-of-function and loss-of-function PIK3R1 phenotypes.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: PIK3R1 gene products (p85α, p55α, and p50α) are essential for class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) signalling.
source: PIK3R1 gene products (p85α, p55α, and p50α) are essential for class IA phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) signalling.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Each of the three PIK3R1 protein products can bind any of three catalytic subunits, p110α, β, and δ.
source: Each of the three protein products can bind any of three catalytic subunits, p110α, β, and δ, encoded by PIK3CA, PIK3CB, and PIK3CD, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: p110α is encoded by PIK3CA.
source: Each of the three protein products can bind any of three catalytic subunits, p110α, β, and δ, encoded by PIK3CA, PIK3CB, and PIK3CD, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: p110β is encoded by PIK3CB.
source: Each of the three protein products can bind any of three catalytic subunits, p110α, β, and δ, encoded by PIK3CA, PIK3CB, and PIK3CD, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: p110δ is encoded by PIK3CD.
source: Each of the three protein products can bind any of three catalytic subunits, p110α, β, and δ, encoded by PIK3CA, PIK3CB, and PIK3CD, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: PIK3R1 products stabilise and inhibit the catalytic subunits in the basal state.
source: This stabilises and inhibits the catalytic subunits in the basal state and confers responsiveness to upstream stimuli including receptor tyrosine kinase activation, enabled by two phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domains shared by all PIK3R1 products (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: PIK3R1 products confer responsiveness to upstream stimuli including receptor tyrosine kinase activation.
source: This stabilises and inhibits the catalytic subunits in the basal state and confers responsiveness to upstream stimuli including receptor tyrosine kinase activation, enabled by two phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domains shared by all PIK3R1 products (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: All PIK3R1 products share two phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domains.
source: This stabilises and inhibits the catalytic subunits in the basal state and confers responsiveness to upstream stimuli including receptor tyrosine kinase activation, enabled by two phosphotyrosine-binding SH2 domains shared by all PIK3R1 products (Fruman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Some PIK3R1 mutations reduce basal inhibition of catalytic subunits, usually due to disruption of the inhibitory inter-SH2 domain.
source: Some PIK3R1 mutations reduce basal inhibition of catalytic subunits, usually due to disruption of the inhibitory inter-SH2 domain, and are found in cancers (Philp et al., 2001) and vascular malformations with overgrowth (Cottrell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PIK3R1 mutations that reduce basal inhibition of catalytic subunits are found in cancers.
source: Some PIK3R1 mutations reduce basal inhibition of catalytic subunits, usually due to disruption of the inhibitory inter-SH2 domain, and are found in cancers (Philp et al., 2001) and vascular malformations with overgrowth (Cottrell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: PIK3R1 mutations that reduce basal inhibition of catalytic subunits are found in vascular malformations with overgrowth.
source: Some PIK3R1 mutations reduce basal inhibition of catalytic subunits, usually due to disruption of the inhibitory inter-SH2 domain, and are found in cancers (Philp et al., 2001) and vascular malformations with overgrowth (Cottrell et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: In cancers and vascular malformations with overgrowth, hyperactivated PI3Kα drives pathological growth.
source: In both diseases, hyperactivated PI3Kα, composed of heterodimers of PIK3R1 products and p110α, drives pathological growth.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an interpretation of the role of PI3Kα in these diseases.

claim: Distinct inter-SH2 domain PIK3R1 mutations, mostly causing skipping of exon 11 and deletion of residues 434–475, hyperactivate PI3Kδ in immune cells.
source: Distinct inter-SH2 domain PIK3R1 mutations, mostly causing skipping of exon 11 and deletion of residues 434–475, hyperactivate PI3Kδ in immune cells, causing highly penetrant monogenic immunodeficiency (Deau et al., 2014; Lucas et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Inter-SH2 domain PIK3R1 mutations that hyperactivate PI3Kδ cause highly penetrant monogenic immunodeficiency.
source: Distinct inter-SH2 domain PIK3R1 mutations, mostly causing skipping of exon 11 and deletion of residues 434–475, hyperactivate PI3Kδ in immune cells, causing highly penetrant monogenic immunodeficiency (Deau et al., 2014; Lucas et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The immunodeficiency caused by PIK3R1 mutations phenocopies the immunodeficiency caused by genetic activation of p110δ itself (APDS1).
source: This phenocopies the immunodeficiency caused by genetic activation of p110δ itself, which is named activated PI3K delta syndrome 1 (APDS1) (Angulo et al., 2013; Lucas et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Features attributable to PI3Kα activation have been described in only a single case of APDS2 to date.
source: Despite ubiquitous PIK3R1 expression, features attributable to PI3Kα activation have been described in only a single case of APDS2 to date (Wentink et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: In the single APDS2 case with PI3Kα activation features, the causal variant (N564K) was a constitutional activating mutation associated with cancer.
source: In that case, the causal variant (N564K) was a constitutional activating mutation associated with cancer rather than one of the common APDS2 variants.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Biochemical studies suggest that apparently selective p110δ activation in APDS2 occurs because APDS2 mutations derepress p110δ more than p110α.
source: Biochemical studies have suggested that apparently selective p110δ activation occurs because APDS2 mutations derepress p110δ, the predominant immune system catalytic subunit, more than p110α, due to differences in the inhibitory contacts between PIK3R1 products and different catalytic subunits (Dornan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Differences in the inhibitory contacts between PIK3R1 products and different catalytic subunits explain differential derepression of p110δ versus p110α by APDS2 mutations.
source: Biochemical studies have suggested that apparently selective p110δ activation occurs because APDS2 mutations derepress p110δ, the predominant immune system catalytic subunit, more than p110α, due to differences in the inhibitory contacts between PIK3R1 products and different catalytic subunits (Dornan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Phenotypic overlap is reported between APDS2 and SHORT syndrome.
source: More surprisingly, phenotypic overlap is reported between APDS2 and SHORT syndrome.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: SHORT syndrome is caused by loss of PI3Kα function due to disruption of the phosphotyrosine-binding C-terminal SH2 domain.
source: SHORT syndrome, named for the characteristic developmental features (short stature, hyperextensibility, hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay), is caused by loss of PI3Kα function due to disruption of the phosphotyrosine-binding C-terminal SH2 domain (Chudasama et al., 2013; Dyment et al., 2013; Thauvin-Robinet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: SHORT syndrome features short stature, insulin resistance, and dysmorphic features.
source: It features short stature, insulin resistance, and dysmorphic features (Avila et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Many people with APDS2 have overt features of SHORT syndrome.
source: In recent years, both individual case reports (Bravo García-Morato et al., 2017; Petrovski et al., 2016; Ramirez et al., 2020; Szczawińska-Popłonyk et al., 2022) and larger case series Elkaim et al., 2016; Jamee et al., 2020; Maccari et al., 2023; Nguyen et al., 2023; Olbrich et al., 2016; Petrovski et al., 2016 have established that many people with APDS2 have overt features of SHORT syndrome
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Linear growth impairment is common in APDS2, but not in APDS1.
source: while, more generally, linear growth impairment is common in APDS2, but not in APDS1.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a clinical observation.

claim: Mice with knock-in of the common causal APDS2 mutation in Pik3r1 show impaired linear growth.
source: These clinical observations are bolstered by the impaired linear growth and increased in utero mortality reported in mice with knock-in of the common causal APDS2 mutation in Pik3r1 (Nguyen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Mice with knock-in of the common causal APDS2 mutation in Pik3r1 show increased in utero mortality.
source: These clinical observations are bolstered by the impaired linear growth and increased in utero mortality reported in mice with knock-in of the common causal APDS2 mutation in Pik3r1 (Nguyen et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: All people with SHORT-APDS2 overlap syndromes have well-established activating PIK3R1 mutations in the inter-SH2 domain implicated in APDS2.
source: All people with SHORT-APDS2 overlap syndromes have well-established activating PIK3R1 mutations in the inter-SH2 domain implicated in APDS2, but none have characteristic SHORT synfdrome mutations, which are usually in the C-terminal SH2 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a clinical observation.

claim: No patient with a classical SHORT syndrome mutation has been shown to have immunodeficiency.
source: Conversely, no patient with a classical SHORT syndrome mutation has been shown to have immunodeficiency.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a clinical observation.

claim: Regulatory and catalytic subunits stabilise each other upon binding.
source: Regulatory and catalytic subunits stabilise each other upon binding (Brachmann et al., 2005; Yu et al., 1998), and only regulatory subunit monomers are stable enough to be detected in mammalian cells (Yu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Only regulatory subunit monomers are stable enough to be detected in mammalian cells.
source: Regulatory and catalytic subunits stabilise each other upon binding (Brachmann et al., 2005; Yu et al., 1998), and only regulatory subunit monomers are stable enough to be detected in mammalian cells (Yu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Molar excess of regulatory subunits over catalytic subunits gives rise to free regulatory subunits that compete with holoenzyme for phosphotyrosine binding.
source: Molar excess of regulatory subunits over catalytic subunits gives rise to free regulatory subunits that compete with holoenzyme for phosphotyrosine binding (Ueki et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The 'free p85' model has been invoked to explain increased insulin sensitivity on knockout or reduction of p85α alone.
source: This has been invoked to explain increased insulin sensitivity on knockout or reduction of p85α alone (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2002), of p55α and p50α (Chen et al., 2004) or of all Pik3r1 products (Fruman et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The 'free p85' model has been contested by some reports suggesting no excess p85.
source: The 'free p85' model has been contested by some reports suggesting no excess p85 (Geering et al., 2007; Zhao et al., 2006)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Most observations suggest that monomeric p85α can be seen in vivo in some tissues.
source: however most observations, including some made recently using in vivo tagging and pulldown of PI3K components (Tsolakos et al., 2018), suggest that monomeric p85α can be seen in vivo in some tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Truncated p85α was expressed in APDS2 fibroblasts, but at a much lower protein level than full-length wild-type p85α.
source: We found that truncated p85α was expressed, but at a much lower protein level than full-length wild-type (WT) p85α (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1A.

claim: No increase in basal or insulin-stimulated AKT phosphorylation was seen in APDS2 cells compared to cells from WT volunteers or from people with PROS.
source: Despite this, no increase in basal or insulin-stimulated AKT phosphorylation was seen in APDS2 cells compared to cells from WT volunteers or from people with PROS and activating PIK3CA mutations H1047L or H1047R (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1.

claim: Both p110α and p110δ were easily detectable in control dermal fibroblasts.
source: We found that both p110α and p110δ were easily detectable in control dermal fibroblasts
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1.

claim: p110δ was almost absent in APDS2 fibroblasts compared to controls.
source: however p110δ was almost absent in APDS2 fibroblasts compared to controls, with lower levels also seen in PROS cells (Figure 1A and D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: p110α was unchanged in APDS2 cells but modestly increased in PROS cells.
source: p110α was unchanged in APDS2 cells but modestly increased in PROS cells (Figure 1A and E, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Any ability of the APDS2 PIK3R1 variant in skin cells to activate PI3K may be overcome by reduced protein levels of p110δ.
source: Collectively these findings suggest that any ability of the APDS2 PIK3R1 variant in skin cells to activate PI3K may be overcome by reduced protein levels of p110δ, likely through reduced binding and/or reduced stabilisation of p110δ by the mutant regulatory subunit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Overexpression of oncogenic H1047R p110α strongly increased basal Akt phosphorylation in 3T3-L1 preadipocytes.
source: As expected, overexpression of oncogenic H1047R p110α strongly increased basal Akt phosphorylation (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and C) with no additional increase on insulin stimulation (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of the APDS2 ΔEx11 p85α did not increase basal PI3Kα signalling in 3T3-L1 preadipocytes.
source: Surprisingly, however, not only did overexpression of the APDS2 ΔEx11 p85α not increase basal PI3Kα signalling, but it also potently inhibited insulin-induced Akt phosphorylation, consistent with a strong dominant negative action on pathway activation (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of the APDS2 ΔEx11 p85α potently inhibited insulin-induced Akt phosphorylation in 3T3-L1 preadipocytes.
source: Surprisingly, however, not only did overexpression of the APDS2 ΔEx11 p85α not increase basal PI3Kα signalling, but it also potently inhibited insulin-induced Akt phosphorylation, consistent with a strong dominant negative action on pathway activation (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of the APDS2 ΔEx11 p85α is consistent with a strong dominant negative action on pathway activation.
source: Surprisingly, however, not only did overexpression of the APDS2 ΔEx11 p85α not increase basal PI3Kα signalling, but it also potently inhibited insulin-induced Akt phosphorylation, consistent with a strong dominant negative action on pathway activation (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Overexpressing WT p85α mildly reduced insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation in 3T3-L1 preadipocytes.
source: Overexpressing WT p85α mildly reduced insulin-stimulated Akt phosphorylation (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C), although WT p85α was not expressed to as high a level as ΔEx11 p85a.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Overexpression of the ΔEx11 variant severely impaired adipocyte differentiation.
source: In keeping with impaired PI3Kα activity, overexpression of the ΔEx11 variant also severely impaired adipocyte differentiation, assessed by triglyceride accumulation in response to a standard differentiation protocol (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Overexpression of SHORT syndrome variants R649W and Y657X severely impaired adipocyte differentiation.
source: A similar effect was seen on overexpressing SHORT syndrome variants R649W and Y657X (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ΔEx11 holoenzyme could only be made in small amounts under identical conditions and was unstable on storage.
source: Wild-type and SHORT syndrome mutant holoenzymes were successfully purified for in vitro assay, but despite multiple attempts, ΔEx11 holoenzyme could only be made in small amounts under identical conditions, and moreover was unstable on storage, precluding further study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing in vitro enzyme assays.

claim: Instability of in vitro synthesised ΔEx11 holoenzyme was previously reported.
source: Such instability of in vitro synthesised ΔEx11 holoenzyme was previously reported (Dornan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by a citation.

claim: p85α R649W showed severely reduced phosphotyrosine-stimulated activity in complex with p110α.
source: Also in keeping with previous reports (Chudasama et al., 2013; Dornan et al., 2017; Dornan et al., 2020), p85α R649W showed severely reduced phosphotyrosine-stimulated activity in complex with p110α, with highly significant but lesser loss of function seen for Y657X and E489K (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: p85α Y657X showed highly significant but lesser loss of function than R649W in complex with p110α.
source: Also in keeping with previous reports (Chudasama et al., 2013; Dornan et al., 2017; Dornan et al., 2020), p85α R649W showed severely reduced phosphotyrosine-stimulated activity in complex with p110α, with highly significant but lesser loss of function seen for Y657X and E489K (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: p85α E489K showed highly significant but lesser loss of function than R649W in complex with p110α.
source: Also in keeping with previous reports (Chudasama et al., 2013; Dornan et al., 2017; Dornan et al., 2020), p85α R649W showed severely reduced phosphotyrosine-stimulated activity in complex with p110α, with highly significant but lesser loss of function seen for Y657X and E489K (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No increase in basal activity was seen for any SHORT syndrome variant in complex with p110α.
source: No increase in basal activity was seen for any variant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing in vitro enzyme assays.

claim: All SHORT syndrome variants impaired phosphotyrosine-stimulated activity of PI3Kβ.
source: We also assessed whether any of the SHORT syndrome variants affect function of PI3Kβ and found that all variants impaired phosphotyrosine-stimulated activity of PI3Kβ.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For PI3Kβ, impairment was less for p85α Y657X than for R649W, and only very mild for E489K.
source: Again, this impairment was less for p85α Y657X than for R649W, and in this case only very mild for E489K (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For PI3Kδ, p85α R649W conferred severe loss of function.
source: For PI3Kδ, p85α R649W conferred severe loss of function, as for other isoforms (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The absence of immunodeficiency in SHORT syndrome is not accounted for by selective inhibition of PI3Kα function by causal mutations.
source: suggesting that the absence of immunodeficiency in SHORT syndrome is not accounted for by selective inhibition of PI3Kα function by causal mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: p85α was easily detected in anti-p110α immunoprecipitates from all cell lines at baseline.
source: p85α was easily detected in anti-p110α immunoprecipitates from all cell lines at baseline (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: No increase in p110α levels was seen on conditional overexpression of WT or R649W p85α.
source: No increase in p110α levels was seen on conditional overexpression of WT or R649W p85α.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: All p110α is bound to p85α before overexpression.
source: Given the known instability of monomeric p110α, this suggests that all p110α is bound to p85α before overexpression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: For cells overexpressing the SHORT syndrome-associated p85α Y657X, the truncated variant was strongly co-immunoprecipitated.
source: For cells overexpressing the SHORT syndrome-associated p85α Y657X, the truncated variant was strongly co-immunoprecipitated, accounting for nearly all of the p85α signal in anti-p110α immunoprecipitate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: p85α Y657X demonstrates preserved binding of p110α by mutant p85α.
source: This demonstrates preserved binding of p110α by mutant p85α (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Truncated p85α ΔEx11 was easily detected in cell lysates before immunoprecipitation and in supernatant after immunoprecipitation.
source: In sharp contrast, although truncated p85α ΔEx11 was easily detected in cell lysates before immunoprecipitation and in supernatant after immunoprecipitation (arrowed in Figure 4), no truncated p85α ΔEx11 was seen in p110α immunoprecipitates
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: No truncated p85α ΔEx11 was seen in p110α immunoprecipitates.
source: In sharp contrast, although truncated p85α ΔEx11 was easily detected in cell lysates before immunoprecipitation and in supernatant after immunoprecipitation (arrowed in Figure 4), no truncated p85α ΔEx11 was seen in p110α immunoprecipitates, and no change in p110α expression was detected (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: No change in p110α expression was detected upon overexpression of p85α ΔEx11.
source: In sharp contrast, although truncated p85α ΔEx11 was easily detected in cell lysates before immunoprecipitation and in supernatant after immunoprecipitation (arrowed in Figure 4), no truncated p85α ΔEx11 was seen in p110α immunoprecipitates, and no change in p110α expression was detected (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The truncated APDS2 causal variant does not supplant endogenous, full-length p85α binding to p110α, despite overexpression.
source: This suggests that this truncated APDS2 causal variant does not supplant endogenous, full-length p85α binding to p110α, despite overexpression.

claim: The data argues against destabilisation of p110α as the mechanism of the observed dominant negative activity of p85α ΔEx11.
source: This argues against destabilisation of p110α as the mechanism of the observed dominant negative activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Overexpression of WT p85α had no effect on basal or insulin-induced p110α recruitment to Irs1.
source: Overexpression of WT p85α had no effect on basal or insulin-induced p110α recruitment to Irs1 (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Overexpression of either p85α R649W or Y657X sharply reduced insulin-stimulated p110α recruitment to Irs1.
source: In contrast, overexpression of either p85α R649W or Y657X sharply reduced insulin-stimulated p110α recruitment to Irs1 on insulin stimulation (Figure 5A and B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: p85α R649W was not recruited to Irs1.
source: In keeping with the inability of the R649W cSH2 domain to bind phosphotyrosines, p85α R649W was also not recruited to Irs1
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Overexpression of Y657X increased stimulated but not basal p85α recruitment to Irs1.
source: while overexpression of Y657X increased stimulated but not basal p85α recruitment (Figure 5A and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: For R649W, the signalling defect is a pure defect in PI3K holoenzyme recruitment.
source: This suggests a pure defect in PI3K holoenzyme recruitment for R649W.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: For Y657X, the signalling defect may have mixed mechanisms, with reduced activation by phosphotyrosine coupled to increased abundance of monomeric mutant p85α.
source: For Y657X the signalling defect may have mixed mechanisms, with reduced activation by phosphotyrosine seen in in vitro studies coupled to increased abundance of monomeric mutant p85α, leading to recruitment of non p110α-bound mutant p85α to Irs1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: Overexpression of p85a ΔEx11 abolished p110α recruitment to Irs1.
